paragraphs.heading: What a mushroom is
paragraphs.text: A mushroom is the fleshy part of a fungus that carries spores, called its fruiting body, and it usually rises above the ground on soil or another food source. It grows out of the mycelium, the mass of thread-like hyphae that make up the fungus, which lies underground. In good conditions a mushroom can swell quickly. The word is a common label for fungal fruiting bodies big enough to see, not a precise scientific category. About 14,000 kinds of mushroom have been described.

paragraphs.heading: Gills and spores
paragraphs.text: Most mushrooms belong to the basidiomycetes and have gills, the blade-like parts under the cap. The gills make microscopic spores, which help the fungus spread. These spores, called basidiospores, are shot off structures named basidia and then drop between the gills through still air. They fall from under the cap as a fine rain of powder.

paragraphs.heading: Reading a spore print
paragraphs.text: Cut the cap off most mushrooms and leave it gills down overnight, and the falling spores leave a powdery pattern that copies the shape of the gills. This pattern is called a spore print, and its color helps both to classify and to identify mushrooms. Prints are most often white, but can be brown, black, purple-brown, pink, yellow or creamy; blue, green and red almost never turn up. Beginners have sometimes mistaken damp water marks on the paper for a white print.

paragraphs.heading: Naming a mushroom
paragraphs.text: Amateur and professional mycologists alike weigh many clues: juices that appear when the mushroom breaks, how it reacts to bruising, smell, taste, shade, habitat, growth habit and season. Tasting and sniffing carry their own risks, because of poisons and allergens. A local field guide can often get you to the genus out in the field, but naming the species takes more effort. Molecular methods are spreading fast, yet most people still use the traditional approach together with a microscope.

paragraphs.heading: From pinhead to button
paragraphs.text: A mushroom begins as a tiny knot less than two millimeters across, called a primordium, which forms within the mycelium on or near the surface it grows on. The primordium swells into a rounded, egg-like mass of woven hyphae called a button. In some mushrooms a cottony layer, the universal veil, wraps around the button. As the mushroom expands, this veil tears and may leave a cup at the base of the stalk or warty patches on the cap. Many mushrooms have no universal veil, so they show neither.

paragraphs.heading: Rings and veils
paragraphs.text: The gills are often hidden behind a second sheet of tissue, the partial veil. When the cap opens out, this veil breaks, and its remains may form a ring around the stalk or hang as scraps from the cap's edge. In some Amanita species the ring looks like a skirt, while in many Lepiota species it looks more like a collar. In Cortinarius only faint traces remain of a cobweb-like veil called a cortina.

paragraphs.heading: Mushrooms off the usual pattern
paragraphs.text: The lobster mushroom is a Russula or Lactarius mushroom that a parasitic fungus has twisted out of shape. The result is oddly formed and red, much like a boiled lobster. Other fungi called mushrooms have no gills: some have pores underneath, and others, such as the hedgehog mushroom, have spines. Puffballs, stinkhorns, cup fungi, bracket fungi, coral fungi and jelly fungi have all been called mushrooms too.
